expectations.text: Frames the issue: civil vs criminal, substantive vs procedural, area of law

Matches SKILL.md's four-step framing.

expectations.text: Uses the Cartwheel method or keyword brainstorming
expectations.evidence: Section 2 'Search terms (Cartwheel)' table uses exactly the skill's nine categories (major words, broader, narrower, synonyms, antonyms, closely related, procedural, agencies, long shots) plus Boolean queries; the 'runs out of patience at the index' quote matches the skill.

expectations.text: Points to secondary sources first (e.g. practice guides, Am. Jur., form books) then primary law
expectations.evidence: Section 3 'Start with secondary sources (Ch. 2 and 4)' before Section 4 'Primary law': Nolo.com/Everybody's Guide to Small Claims Court, NY practice guide or encyclopedia (NY Jurisprudence), UCC treatise; 'state-specific source is almost always best' matches the skill's state-encyclopedia note. Then NY UCC, federal regs, small claims acts, cases.

expectations.text: Mentions checking that law is still good (Shepardize/KeyCite or updates/pocket parts)

expectations.text: Mentions small claims court and/or when to hire a lawyer; notes it's not legal advice

expectations.text: Gives rules for reading statutes (e.g. read definitions, every word matters, cross-references)
expectations.evidence: Part 2 'Nolo's seven rules for reading a statute' lists all seven in the book's order and wording (read three times then again; 'and'/'or'; every word and punctuation has meaning; consistent with related statutes incl. definitions section; criminal statutes strictly; further purpose; make sense, with the correct California '$100 a day' -> 'up to $100' example), plus 'Follow every cross-reference' and 'court interpretations are part of the statute'. All match SKILL references.

expectations.text: Explains holding vs dicta in cases
expectations.evidence: Part 3 'Holding versus dicta: the holding is the ruling needed to decide the case. Dicta are side comments... aren't binding (except... US Supreme Court)'; also headnotes not law, majority/plurality only. Matches skill Ch 7.

expectations.text: Explains binding vs persuasive precedent
expectations.evidence: Part 3 'Is it binding on your small claims court?': trial-level decisions don't create binding precedent; state appellate courts bind; 'Out-of-state cases are only persuasive'; analysis step 3 'binding or only persuasive'.
